properties.foundation_analysis:
The West End of Edinburgh rests upon Early Carboniferous sedimentary bedrock of the Strathclyde Group (sandstones, siltstones, and oil-shales) overlying glacial till, shaped into classic crag-and-tail landforms by Quaternary glacial flows. In the far left background rises the basaltic volcanic plug of Castle Rock and the distant silhouette of Arthur's Seat / Salisbury Crags (Carboniferous volcanic neck and basaltic sill system).
- Primary Architectural Lithics: High-quartz fine-grained Craigleith Sandstone (Carboniferous age, pale blonde to warm buff-grey) forming the monumental Gothic fabric of St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral, complemented by Dunmore and Hailes quarry sandstones across the surrounding Victorian residential terraces.
- Mortar Chemistry: Traditional hot-mixed Scottish non-hydraulic and feebly hydraulic lime mortars with coarse grit sand, providing moisture breathability across dense ashlar joints.
- Subterranean Hydrology: Natural south-to-north/east gravitational drainage toward the Water of Leith basin, regulated by subterranean vaulted cellars and stone storm-culvert networks.

properties.primary_surfacing: Engineered roadway and paved pedestrian curbs
properties.wear_characteristics: Authentic environmental patina and drainage grading

properties.botanical_analysis:
- Urban Green Infrastructure: Clustered private garden enclosures, cathedral grounds, and street verges populated by mature, organic deciduous trees:
  - *Acer pseudoplatanus* (Sycamore / Scottish Plane) with broad, multi-lobed deep green foliage and mottled bark.
  - *Ulmus glabra* (Wych Elm) and *Tilia x europaea* (Common Lime) forming full, rounded organic leafy canopies.
  - Manicured ground cover of perennial turf grass (*Poa pratensis*, *Festuca rubra*) within private communal gardens and churchyard verges.
- Disambiguation: All low-poly 3D photogrammetry green meshes are resolved strictly into branching botanical wood and discrete leafy canopy volumes.

properties.architectural_summary:
- Primary Landmark (Foreground/Midground Left): St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott (Early Gothic Revival, consecrated 1879). Features a monumental central crossing tower and soaring stone spire (reaching 84 meters / 275 feet), twin western towers with matching spires (the "Barbara and Mary" spires added 1913–1917), clerestory lancet fenestration, flying buttresses, ribbed stone vaulting profiles, and a faceted south chapter house.
- Surrounding Urban Fabric: High Victorian and late Georgian New Town/West End residential terraces (Manor Place, Eglinton Crescent, Grosvenor Crescent, and Palmerston Place). Distinctive 3.5 to 4.5 storey uniform residential blocks (floor-to-ceiling heights ~3.8m on piano nobile, terminating in steep double-pitched slate roofs with lead flat tops, rhythmic ashlar chimney stacks with clay chimney pots, and dormer attics).
- Distant Urban Texture (Midground & Background Right): Continuous Georgian neoclassical grid extending toward the city centre, punctuated by modern institutional flat-roof infills (rectilinear curtain-wall glass and precast concrete floor slabs) and Victorian drum-domed churches and public halls.
- Planar Rectification: All photogrammetric distortions, leaning vertical spires, and warped terrace facades are plumbed to absolute gravitational vertical (0.0° deviation). Roof ridges, stringcourses, and cornice lines are rectified into crisp, continuous horizontal planes.
